title: Ashes and India Series Power Cricket Australia to Record A$601 Million Revenue
excerpt: A home Ashes and India's white-ball tour turned an A$11.3 million loss into an A$81.8 million surplus, even as two-day Tests cost CA A$20 million and lean years loom.
body:
• Cricket Australia posted record revenue of A$601.1 million ($423 million) and a net surplus of A$81.8 million ($57 million) for 2025-26, reversing an A$11.3 million loss the year before.
  • The home Ashes and India's white-ball tour generated record media, commercial and match-day revenue; the Ashes drew 859,580 spectators over 18 days.
  • Two-day Tests in Perth and Melbourne cost CA about A$20 million in lost revenue, chief executive Todd Greenberg confirmed.
  • CA forecasts losses for the next two financial years as media rights revenue declines cyclically, and up to three states may soon vote on Big Bash League privatisation.

Media rights agreements for the Ashes and a limited-overs series against India have helped Cricket Australia post a record revenue of A$601.1 million ($423 million) and a net surplus of A$81.8 million ($57 million), the governing body said on Wednesday. The 2025-26 result, reported by the Associated Press, reflected strong commercial performance, record audiences and the success of its international season — a sharp swing from the net loss of A$11.3 million recorded in 2024-25.

The India and Ashes effect

CA said the men's home Test series against England and the white-ball series against India generated record levels of media, commercial and match-day revenue. Attendance records fell with them: the Ashes attracted 859,580 spectators over 18 days, an average of 47,754 a day. On the field, Australia's men retained the Ashes with a 4-1 home victory, and the women's team won a seventh ICC T20 World Cup, beating England in the final at Lord's. In the India series last October and November, Australia won the ODI series 2-1 and India won the T20 series 2-1.

The numbers underline a structural fact of world cricket: an India tour is the single most valuable property most boards can host. India's white-ball visit, layered on top of an Ashes summer, turned what CA had braced for as a rebuilding year into the strongest financial result in its history.

The costs hiding inside the record

The surplus came despite a self-inflicted wound. Chief executive Todd Greenberg confirmed that the fallout from the two-day Tests in Perth and Melbourne cost CA about $20 million in lost revenue, according to AAP — ticket refunds, lost hospitality and broadcast value from matches that ended before the weekend crowds arrived. Greenberg also warned of "significant" financial losses over the next two years because of international scheduling and a cyclical decline in media revenue. CA itself said losses are forecast for 2026-27 and 2027-28 "due to a cyclical decline in media rights and match revenues in line with the international touring schedule."

"We're still working our way through that, but my guess is at the moment that certainly Victoria's second team and Tasmania are particularly weighing up what that looks like."

— Todd Greenberg, Cricket Australia chief executive, on BBL privatisation

Privatisation vote and a changing of the guard

The annual general meeting also reset CA's leadership and its biggest strategic fight. Chairman Mike Baird formally handed over to former Test opener David Boon as interim chairman, a month after announcing he would leave; Baird quit after his home state association, New South Wales, refused to back him over privatisation. Ed Cowan, also a former Test opener, replaced Baird as the NSW representative on the board. Greenberg said up to three states — Victoria, Tasmania and Western Australia are actively engaged — could vote on Big Bash League privatisation within six to eight weeks, with the Melbourne Renegades seen as the club most likely to be privately owned for the 2027-28 season. Private investment in BBL teams is CA's chosen hedge against the lean years it has just forecast, a model borrowed from the IPL's franchise economics.

What comes next

Australia's men's team is in South Africa for a Test series now and will play England in a white-ball series at home starting November 13 before hosting New Zealand for four Tests from December 9 to January 8. The men's team then heads to India for a five-Test series starting January 21 at Nagpur — the return fixture of the rivalry that just filled CA's coffers, this time filling the BCCI's. For Indian fans and the diaspora audiences who made the white-ball tour a record draw, the financial results confirm their commercial weight: when India tours, the host board's balance sheet transforms.
